items.quip: California plus Mexico on the border; Mexicali mirrors it across the line.
items.title: Calexico, California
items.extract: Calexico is a city in southern Imperial County, California, United States. As of the 2020 census, Calexico had a population of 38,633. Situated on the Mexican border, it is linked economically with the much larger city of Mexicali, the capital of the Mexican state of Baja California. It is about 122 miles (196 km) east of San Diego and 62 miles (100 km) west of Yuma, Arizona. Calexico, along with six other incorporated Imperial County cities, forms part of the larger populated area known as the Imperial Valley. First explored by Europeans in the 18th century, Calexico began as a small tent community which was ultimately incorporated in 1908.

items.title: Rough and Ready, California
items.description: Census-designated place in California, United States
items.extract: Rough and Ready is a census-designated place in Nevada County, California, United States. It is located west of Grass Valley, California, approximately 62 miles (100 km) from Sacramento. The population was 905 at the 2020 census. It has frequently been noted on lists of unusual place names.

prompts.text: Name an animal with horns or antlers

items.quip: Only wild bovid with four horns, all on one small Indian head.
items.title: Four-horned antelope
items.description: Small species of antelope from Asia
items.extract: The four-horned antelope, also called chousingha, is a small bovid antelope native to central, South and Western India, along with a smaller population in Nepal. The sole member of the genus Tetracerus, the chousingha was first scientifically described in 1816 by French zoologist Henri Marie Ducrotay de Blainville. Three regional subspecies are currently recognised. The four-horned antelope has a yellowish-tan, sometimes reddish or goldenrod coat. It is slender with thin legs and a short tail. It stands nearly 55–64 cm (22–25 in) at the shoulder and weighs about 17–22 kg (37–49 lb). Its four horns are unique among antelopes and distinguish it from most other bovids. The longer pair of straight, spike-like horns is atop its head between the ears, while the other, shorter pair is on the forehead; its posterior horns are always longer than the anterior horns, which may even present as merely fur-covered "studs". While the posterior horns measure 8–12 cm (3.1–4.7 in), the anterior ones are usually 2–5 cm (0.79–1.97 in) long.

items.quip: Bhutan's national animal, built like a goat crossed with a moose.
items.title: Takin
items.extract: The takin ; is a large species of ungulate of the subfamily Caprinae found in the eastern Himalayas. It includes three subspecies, the Mishmi takin, the golden takin, and the Bhutan takin, and is closely related to the Tibetan takin (B. tibetana)

prompts.text: Name a Spanish or Portuguese dish

items.quip: Sausage invented by Portuguese Jews to fake eating pork under the Inquisition.
items.title: Alheira
items.extract: Alheira, or Tabafeia in Mirandese, is a type of Portuguese sausage, made with meats and bread.

items.quip: Azorean stew buried in volcanic ground and cooked by the earth.
items.title: Cocido
items.description: Dish made of various meats and vegetables of Spanish and Portuguese origins
items.extract: Cocido or cozido is a traditional stew eaten as a main dish in Spain, Portugal, Brazil and other Hispanophone and Lusophone countries.

items.quip: Snorkel-nosed aquatic mole of Pyrenean and Russian streams.
items.title: Desman
items.extract: Desmans are aquatic insectivores of the tribe Desmanini in the mole family, Talpidae.

items.quip: Only aquatic marsupial; its pouch seals watertight when diving.
items.title: Water opossum
items.extract: The water opossum, also locally known as the yapok, is a marsupial of the family Didelphidae. It is the only monotypic species of its genus, Chironectes. This semiaquatic creature is found in and near freshwater streams and lakes from Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina and is the most aquatic living marsupial. It is also the only extant marsupial species in which both sexes have a pouch. The now extinct thylacine, commonly referred to as the Tasmanian tiger, also exhibited this trait.

items.quip: Desert mouse that hunts scorpions and howls at the moon.
items.title: Northern grasshopper mouse
items.extract: The northern grasshopper mouse is a North American carnivorous rodent of the family Cricetidae. It ranges over much of the western part of the continent, from southern Saskatchewan and central Washington to Tamaulipas in northeast Mexico.

items.quip: Hunts birds and rodents; drinks no blood despite the name.
items.title: Big-eared woolly bat
items.description: Species of mammals belonging to the New World leaf-nosed bat family
items.extract: The big-eared woolly bat or (Peters's) woolly false vampire bat is a species of bat, belonging to the family Phyllostomidae.

items.quip: Deus Ex and Thief defined it; critics adore it, publishers fear it.
items.title: Immersive sim
items.extract: An immersive sim (simulation) is a video game genre that emphasizes player choice. Its core defining trait is the use of simulated systems that respond to a variety of player actions, which combined with a comparatively broad array of player abilities allow the game to support varied and creative solutions to problems as well as emergent gameplay beyond what has been explicitly designed by the developer. This definition is not to be confused with game systems which allow player choice in a confined sense or systems which allow players to easily escape consequences of their choices.

prompts.text: Name a street suffix (like Street or Avenue)

items.quip: Tucson's diagonal street-avenue hybrid, abbreviated STRA by the USPS.
items.title: Stravenue
items.description: Road designation particular to Tucson, Arizona
items.extract: A stravenue is a type of road particular to Tucson, Arizona, United States. A stravenue runs "diagonally between and intersects a Street and an Avenue." By convention in Tucson, streets run east–west while avenues run north–south. However, in a few areas of Tucson, primarily around the central part of the city, which is divided by railroad tracks running diagonally from southeast to northwest, builders created small subdivisions of roads and houses that also are laid out on a diagonal basis rather than the normal east–west or north–south. Most of these subdivisions are located near either Benson Highway or Aviation Highway, which also run southeast to northwest.
